title: Exact stationary performance of the $M/G/k$ queue
short_statement: Exact special cases and stationary samplers exist for FCFS multiserver queues. Can general service-time inputs yield efficiently computable stationary probabilities with certified errors?
open_problem: Develop a broadly applicable exact characterization and efficient certified numerical evaluation of stationary FCFS M/G/k probabilities under an explicit input model for the service distribution, or prove a matching computational obstruction. A mean bound or stationary sampler alone does not settle this target.
background: The $M/G/k$ queue is one of the oldest and most natural unsolved models in queueing theory. Poisson arrivals are routed to the first available one of $k$ identical FCFS servers, and service times have a general distribution. When $k=1$, the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula gives a classical exact transform for waiting time. When service times are exponential, the $M/M/k$ birth-death chain is exactly solvable. But for $k\ge2$ and general service times, the Markov state must include residual service times of all busy servers, destroying the one-dimensional transform structure of $M/G/1$. Decades of work provide approximations, special cases, phase-type numerical methods, continuity results, bounds, and heavy-traffic formulas, but no broadly tractable exact characterization comparable to the single-server formula. This is a clean mathematical open problem, not a modelling gap: the model is fixed and classical.
full_statement:
Consider a stationary FCFS $M/G/k$ queue with $k\ge2$ identical unit-speed servers, Poisson arrival rate $\lambda$, iid service time $S\sim G$ independent of arrivals, and load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb E S/k<1$. Let $N_{\rm sys}$ count all jobs in the system, $Q_{\rm wait}$ count only jobs waiting, and $W$ be the delay before service of an arriving job. Residual service times are part of the Markov state.

The target is an exact characterization, together with a certified numerical procedure, for quantities such as $\mathbb P(W>x)$ or $\mathbb P(N_{\rm sys}=j)$ at specified $x\ge0$ and integer $j\ge0$. A useful result must define how $G$ is supplied (for example, finite rational support, a phase-type representation, or a distribution oracle with explicit tail bounds), return errors at most a requested $\varepsilon>0$, and bound its computational cost. An impossibility theorem must likewise fix the input and output model.

The remaining open problem is a broadly applicable, computationally tractable theory beyond special distributions and formal infinite-dimensional balance equations. An exact stationary sample, a mean bound, and a deterministic certified probability calculation are different outputs. Mean-delay claims require additional integrability assumptions; finite mean service alone is not a universal finite-mean-delay assumption.
known_results:
The single-server Pollaczek-Khinchine theory and exponential-service Erlang formulas are exact benchmarks. Phase-type services permit matrix-analytic methods on a countably infinite level process, not generally a finite CTMC. Tijms, van Hoorn, and Federgruen (1981) give practical steady-state approximations. Gupta, Harchol-Balter, Dai, and Zwart (2010) show limitations of using only two service-time moments. Gupta and Osogami (2011) study extremal mean-waiting-time bounds under moment information. Perfect-simulation results address sampling rather than automatically giving a fast, certified numerical distribution.

Hong (arXiv:2510.11015v3, revised August 22, 2026), Theorem 1 and equation (8), gives the bound $\mathbb E Q_{\rm wait}\le R_s^{\max}/(1-\rho)$ for the Poisson-arrival specialization, where $\mu=1/\mathbb E S$ and $R_s^{\max}=\sup_{t:\mathbb P(\mu S\ge t)>0}\mathbb E[\mu S-t\mid\mu S\ge t]$. It assumes bounded mean residual service, non-lattice service, and Assumption 3 on positive Harris recurrence and convergence of mean queue lengths for the auxiliary modified queues. For NBUE service satisfying those assumptions, $R_s^{\max}=1$, hence $\mathbb E Q_{\rm wait}\le1/(1-\rho)$. Jobs in service are excluded from this bound.

Remaining open problem. These sharper nonasymptotic bounds do not provide an exact general stationary distribution or a certified efficient computation for arbitrary $G$.

progress.summary: A revised 2026 preprint gives interpretable nonasymptotic FCFS mean-queue bounds under explicit assumptions. Exact efficient stationary-distribution computation remains a separate question.

counterexample_rationale: This is an exact-characterization problem for a continuum of service distributions. Finite examples can refute approximations but cannot by themselves prove impossibility of an exact method.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can discover transform identities, numerical patterns, and hard service-time distributions for approximations. A resolution likely needs analytic queueing theory or a formal computational-complexity obstruction.

literature.synthesis: The computational target must be separated from existence of a stationary law and from sampling it. The newer leave-one-out bound supplies useful numerical control for light-tailed distributions, but bounds only a mean and carries regularity assumptions on auxiliary queues. General probability computation still needs an explicit distribution input model, a truncation or approximation certificate, and a runtime guarantee. The statement no longer confuses queue length with total population or phase-type matrix analysis with a finite-state chain.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Look for state-space reductions based on workload vectors, symmetric residual-life measures, or transform equations. For impossibility, formalize an input model for $G$ and show exact performance encodes a hard analytic or computational problem.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A proposed formula must specialize correctly to $M/G/1$, $M/M/k$, deterministic service, and phase-type service, and it must specify how arbitrary service distributions are represented as input. A numerical method should include certified truncation or discretization error bounds; otherwise it is an approximation, not a resolution of the exact-performance problem. A claimed impossibility result must define the computational model carefully enough that it does not rule out known exact special cases or perfect-simulation algorithms.

where_posed.text: Computational tractability of general M/G/c steady-state probabilities is discussed by Tijms, van Hoorn, and Federgruen (1981). The certified-algorithm formulation is editorial.
where_posed.location: Discussion of exact computation versus approximations.
